name: Anker 737 PowerCore 24K Power Bank
summary: The best single power bank for an outage drawer: phone charges for a family member for days, plus real laptop support.
verdict: The Anker 737, sold as the PowerCore 24K, is the power bank we would put in a drawer for outages if we could only have one. Anker rates it at 24,000mAh, which works out to somewhere around 86-89 watt-hours, about as large as a power bank can be while staying under the 100Wh limit airlines allow without approval. In practical terms that is three to four full charges for a typical smartphone, or a meaningful top-up for a laptop. What sets it apart from cheaper 20,000mAh banks is output: Anker lists USB-C Power Delivery up to 140W, so it can charge a large laptop at close to full speed instead of trickling, and it refills itself quickly when power briefly comes back, which matters in a rolling outage. The built-in display showing remaining charge removes the guesswork of four blinking dots. The trade-off is heft; it is a dense brick, not something you forget is in your pocket.

name: Anker PowerCore 10000 Power Bank
summary: A cheap, proven pocket bank: buy one for each person in the household and keep them charged.
verdict: Not every charger has to be the biggest. The PowerCore 10000 has been one of the best-known small power banks for years because it does one thing simply: it carries roughly 36-37 watt-hours in a package about the size of a deck of cards, enough to refill a typical phone once and get well into a second charge. That is the right amount for a school bag, a car glovebox or the nightstand of someone who does not want to share the big bank. In an outage, several small banks often beat one large one, because a single shared pack becomes a bottleneck, and at this size you can afford one per person. Know its limits: it is a phone charger, not a laptop charger, and the classic model charges over USB-A at ordinary speed. Anker sells several variants under similar names, some with USB-C, so read the listing for the ports you want.

name: BigBlue 28W Solar Charger
summary: Buy this folding USB panel when you want the most headroom for clouds, short days and a power bank waiting to be filled.
verdict: For years BigBlue’s 28W panel has been a go-to solar powered cell phone charger, and the reason is plain: it has more panel area than the 21W models, so it keeps more in reserve when the sun is weak. BigBlue lists SunPower cells and three USB-A ports. No USB panel passes its full rating through a phone cable, though. The 28W figure describes the cells under ideal lab light; after heat, angle and the 5V regulator, real output commonly settles at about half to two-thirds of it. Even so, this is the strongest tool here for the job that counts, filling a 10,000-20,000mAh bank over a long sunny day. Face it at the sun, plug a bank into it instead of your phone, and top the phone up from the bank in the evening. If a laptop needs USB-C Power Delivery, this panel is the wrong tool; look at a power station instead.

name: Anker PowerPort Solar 21W Solar Charger
summary: The lighter, simpler folding panel for hikers whose main goal is keeping one phone alive.
verdict: Anker’s 21W folder is the lighter option next to the BigBlue, and many backpackers will find it the easier panel to carry. Anker lists two USB-A ports with PowerIQ detection, SunPower cells and a fold-flat fabric body with grommets for hanging it from a pack or tent. What you give up is margin. At a 21W rating, figure on something in the high single digits to low teens of real watts in good sun: enough to charge a phone directly under a clear sky, with less slack when clouds drift through or the sun sits low. The remedy is the one that applies to every panel here: charge a power bank, not the phone. The bank irons out the dips that make a phone stop and restart charging, and it stores the midday harvest for the night. To fill a 20,000mAh bank every day, move up to the 28W class; for a single phone on weekend trips, this panel is plenty.

name: Nekteck 21W Solar Charger
summary: A sensible, inexpensive panel for an emergency kit; pay more only if it will travel with you often.
verdict: Nekteck’s 21W panel offers the Anker’s basic formula for less money: a fold-out fabric panel, two USB-A ports and loops for hanging it in the sun. For an outage kit or a car emergency bag that might come out twice a year, that is the right budget, because the rating and the physics are the same across the class. The savings come out of brand depth and accessory polish, not watts. Set expectations the same way as for any 21W panel: in strong, direct sun it charges one phone, and in mixed weather it fills a bank slowly. Pack it with a charged 10,000mAh power bank and a short cable and you have a solar portable charger that can keep a phone going through a multi-day outage, provided you get a few hours of decent sun. If it will hang off a pack every weekend, the Anker or BigBlue is worth the extra money.

name: BioLite SolarPanel 10+ Solar Charger
summary: The one all-in-one solar charger here with the right panel-to-battery ratio, though it is a small system.
verdict: For the convenience of a solar power bank without the make-believe, the BioLite SolarPanel 10+ is the honest choice. It is not a large battery with a token cell; it is a genuine 10W panel backed by a small 3,200mAh battery. That battery earns its place twice: it keeps current flowing to the phone when a cloud passes, so charging does not cut out, and it stores part of the afternoon’s harvest for later. BioLite adds a kickstand and a little sundial so you can face the panel squarely at the sun, which is the easiest free gain in solar charging. Keep the scale in view, though. Ten watts of panel charges slowly, and 3,200mAh falls short of a full charge for most current phones. It suits a solo hiker on day trips or a short overnight; for longer outings, a 21W or 28W panel with a separate 10,000mAh bank gives you more for similar money.

name: BLAVOR Solar Power Bank 10000mAh
summary: A solid rugged 10,000mAh bank; buy it for the battery and think of the solar cell as an emergency trickle.
verdict: BLAVOR is among the better-known integrated solar power bank brands, and this 10,000mAh model is a fair purchase if you buy it for the right reason. As a power bank it does well: a rugged shell, a wireless charging pad, USB-C plus USB-A, and a flashlight that earns its keep in a blackout. As a solar charger it is weak, and that comes down to physics rather than anything BLAVOR got wrong. A cell the size of a phone makes on the order of a watt or two in ideal sun, while a 10,000mAh bank holds about 37Wh. Even before losses, filling it takes dozens of hours of perfect sun, which in real life means several days on a dashboard or windowsill. Use the cell to win back a little charge when nothing else is available, charge the bank from the wall or a folding panel the rest of the time, and it will serve you well.

name: Anker 335 Power Bank 20000mAh
summary: The battery half of the best solar setup: pair it with any 21W-28W folding panel.
verdict: This is the product that makes a folding panel worth owning. The Anker 335 is a plain 20,000mAh power bank with USB-C and USB-A and no solar cell whatsoever, which is exactly the point. Connected to a 21W or 28W folding panel, it absorbs the midday harvest while you hike or wait out an outage, then charges your phone at full speed over a cable at night, without the start-stop behavior of charging straight from a panel. At roughly 74Wh nominal, a full bank holds about three to four charges for most current phones once conversion losses are counted: a long weekend of normal use, or several days of careful use in an outage. Filling it from empty takes a full sunny day on a 28W panel, so in practice you add a third or half at a time. For laptop charging, step up to a USB-C PD bank instead.
